problem: Omits 'in the world' (the country in the world where service is tightest).
replacement: An American who had spent a long time traveling in Europe once told me, “The English treat their servants with a stiffness and imperiousness of manner which surprise us; but on the other hand the French sometimes treat their attendants with a degree of familiarity or of politeness which we cannot conceive. It looks as if they were afraid to give orders: the posture of the superior and the inferior is ill-maintained.” The remark was just, and I have often made it myself. I have always thought of England as the country in the world where, in our time, the bond of domestic service is drawn tightest, and of France as the country where it is loosest. I have seen masters stand so high, or so low, nowhere else. The Americans fall between these two extremes. That is how the matter looks on the surface. To find the causes behind it, we have to look into it thoroughly.

problem: 'not averse to regard' (litotes) sharpened to 'quite willing'.
replacement: Servants, for their part, are not unwilling to see themselves in the same light, and they sometimes identify with the person of the master, so that they become an appendage of him in their own eyes as well as in his. In aristocracies a servant holds a subordinate position he cannot escape; above him stands another man in a superior rank that he cannot lose. On one side are obscurity, poverty, and lifelong obedience; on the other, equally for life, fame, wealth, and command. The two conditions are always distinct and always close together; the tie between them lasts as long as they do. In this predicament the servant ends by detaching his idea of his interest from his own person. He deserts himself, so to speak, or rather he moves himself into his master’s character and so takes on an imaginary personality. He complacently clothes himself in the wealth of those who command him; he shares their fame, raises himself by their rank, and feeds his mind on borrowed greatness, to which he attaches more importance than those who fully and truly possess it. There is something touching, and at the same time ridiculous, in this strange confusion of two different states of being. When these passions of masters pass into the souls of menials, they take on the natural dimensions of the place they now occupy: they shrink and sink lower. What was pride in the master becomes childish vanity and petty ostentation in the servant. The servants of a great man are usually most punctilious about the marks of respect due to him, and they care more about his slightest privileges than he does himself. In France a few of these old servants of the aristocracy can still be met here and there; they have outlived their race, which will soon vanish altogether with them. In the United States I never saw anyone at all like them. The Americans not only do not know the type; it is hardly possible to make them understand that it ever existed. It is scarcely harder for them to imagine it than for us to form a correct idea of what a slave was among the Romans, or a serf in the Middle Ages. All these men were in fact, though in different degrees, products of the same cause. All of them are withdrawing from our sight and fading into the obscurity of the past, along with the social condition that gave them birth.

I would gladly illustrate all these reflections with the example of the Americans, but for that purpose I must carefully distinguish persons and places. In the South of the Union slavery exists, so everything I have just said is inapplicable there. In the North most servants are either freedmen or the children of freedmen. These people hold a disputed position in public esteem: the laws raise them to the level of their masters, while the customs of the country stubbornly thrust them back down from it. They do not clearly know their own place themselves, and they are almost always either insolent or cowardly. But in the Northern States, especially in New England, there are a certain number of whites who agree, for wages, to yield temporary obedience to the will of their fellow citizens. I have heard that these servants usually carry out the duties of their situation punctually and intelligently, and that without thinking themselves naturally inferior to the person who gives them orders, they submit to obeying him without reluctance. They seem to me to bring into service some of the manly habits that independence and equality produce. Having once chosen a hard way of life, they do not try to escape it by indirect means, and they respect themselves enough not to refuse their master the obedience they freely promised. For their part, masters ask nothing of their servants but faithful and strict performance of the agreement: they do not ask for marks of respect, nor claim their love or devoted attachment; it is enough that, as servants, they are exact and honest. It would not be true, then, to say that in democratic society the relation of servants and masters is disorganized. It is organized on another footing; the rule is different, but there is a rule.

problem: 'the higher its branches have spread' changed to 'the wider'.
replacement: An aristocracy does not die in a single day, as a man does. The aristocratic principle is slowly undermined in people’s opinion before it is attacked in their laws. Long before open war is declared on it, one can see the tie that had held the higher classes to the lower gradually loosen. One class betrays indifference and contempt, the others jealousy and hatred; contact between rich and poor becomes less frequent and less kindly, and rents are raised. This is not the result of a democratic revolution but its sure forerunner; for an aristocracy that has lost the people’s affection, once and for all, is like a tree dead at the root, which the winds tear up the more easily the higher its branches have spread.
